Romance is one of the most structured genres, and it has a formula that determines whatshould be included within the story structure. Romance is a highly popular genre because of its familiarity. Readers can pick up a romance book, and expect to understand the basic outline of what will happen and still be
surprised by how events unfold.

society is defined through the class structures that begin to emerge at the onset of the ball in one of the earliest scenes. In this scene, it is established that Mr Darcy is a wealthy man, as is Mr Bingley, and it begins to become clear that there is a class system and a hierarchy involved.

the meeting occurs when Elizabeth and Mr Darcy have their first interaction. Unfortunately, Mr Darcy chooses to be quite obnoxious within Elizabeth's hearing, and her first impression of him becomes quite negative. Mr Darcy's first impression of her is that her family behaves in an improper manner, and though she is charming, she is "not handsome enough to tempt
me."
, the barrier between Elizabethand Mr Darcy includes their class discrepancies, their initial dislike of each other, Elizabeth's pride, and Mr Darcy's prejudice.

, Mr Darcy falls for Elizabeth, because they keep finding themselves together because of societal events. The more time he spends around her, the more fixated he becomes. Elizabeth, on the other hand, is rather perturbed by his proximity, and wishes he would go away. Her attraction to him takes longer to develop and only emerges when his behaviour towards her family begins to change.

Mr Darcy confesses his feelings for Elizabeth in the rain, and she promptly
rejects him. He is hurt by her uncivil rejection, and asks why. She explains that he confessed his feelings "in spite of his better judgement" and insulted her entire family while he was at it. She lists her reasons for rejecting him, which causes Mr Darcy to reflect on his behaviour, realise that he's acted poorly, and causes him to attempt to resolve the issues. Once he has made as many amends as he can, it's Elizabeth's turn to re-evaluate her judgement of Mr Darcy, and she begins to regret rejecting his proposal.
6. The Moment of Ritual Death: in

, the point of ritual death is a number of accumulated moments that have led to the demise of the relationship between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth. It started with the rejection of the proposal, but the final nail in the coffin of their relationship is Lydia's elopement with Mr Wickham. Poor Elizabeth realises that her family will be ruined by the scandal, and that it will prevent any possibility of a relationship between them, just when she was beginning to believe a relationship with Mr Darcy was something she wanted.

is when Elizabeth learns of Mr Darcy's endeavours to protect her younger sister
and ensure Mr Wickham went through with the elopement. In choosing to protect Elizabeth's family, she realises that Mr Darcy is not the man she originally believed him to be. It is in that moment that Elizabeth realises that she has feelings for Mr Darcy, and a part of her yearns to overturn her rejection of the proposal. Then, she is faced by Lady Catherine De Bourgh, who Mr Darcy's aunt. Lady Catherine demands Elizabeth refuse his proposal, and Elizabeth tells her she will do no such thing. This is the moment of recognition for Mr Darcy, whereby he learns Elizabeth's feelings for him have changed.

is the moment when Mr Darcy returns to propose once more to Elizabeth, believing there's a small possibility she has changed her mind about him. She accepts his proposal and thus ends the romance arc.
